speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. speechtext: I should think that is quite an inaccurate statement. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for St. Denis and the hon. member for Ottawa West asked me certain questions regarding post office practices in the handling of United States coinage. I now have some further information. The question of whether to charge discount on United States coinage is one that has been left to the discretion of our individual district directors in the 14 postal districts of Canada. We have followed this principle so that in this matter, as in many other fields, the local post office practice could conform to general business practice in the area.
Thus, where United States coinage was generally being accepted at par by local merchants and was also being handed out as change at par by them, we have followed this practice. Naturally, if any patron happened to request Canadian coinage or objected to United States coins, he would be given Canadian coinage. This has caused no hardship to patrons, since United States coins were generally in circulation at par. I might add that where we accept United States coins at par, as we generally do across Canada in our 11,500 post offices, unless we used them as change in accordance with normal business practices we would be in danger of becoming the repository of all the United States coins in the area, and thus bearing the total exchange costs with respect to this type of money for the entire community.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Following the action of the Canadian Bankers' Association in discounting coinage when it was included in deposits, in some areas business firms generally began to discount United States coins received from their customers, and in one district of which I know, the Winnipeg district, our post offices were instructed by the district director to follow a similar practice.
However, in accordance with our standard instructions in such cases, the post offices were also instructed in the same memorandum that United States coins were not to be handed out to patrons but deposited in the banks. This practice is always followed by us whenever United States coins are discounted, so there may be no suggestion that we are accepting the money at a discount and then passing it out at face value and profiting thereby.
After about two weeks, when the general business practice in the Winnipeg area reverted to the acceptance of United States coins at par, we followed the same practice and discontinued discounting United States coins when received. Of course this whole question refers to United States coins, which are only a tiny portion of our normal handling of cash.
The best indication I can give hon. members of that fact is in the case of Winnipeg where, during a short period when United States coins were being discounted, and they of course were all deposited in the bank, we received in the Winnipeg stamp depot postal funds totalling $330,421, and of this only $150.05, one twentieth of one per cent, or $1 in $2,200 was in U.S. coins.

When the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were introduced in March, I made an introductory statement outlining some of the activities of this department and giving a general survey. I do not propose to make another such speech at the present time, but there is one matter which has caused some considerable concern, and I think I should take this opportunity- it is really the first I have had-to clear it up.
The need for this statement arises from a Canadian Press dispatch under a Washington dateline which appeared in nearly all our Canadian newspapers. The particular clipping I have is from the Montreal Star of Tuesday, April 19. This dispatch states:
Opening of the St. Lawrence seaway has raised fears among some United States authorities that North American farm lands may be threatened with heavier invasion by foreign crop-damaging beetles, viruses, bugs and other pests and disease.
One of these experts, recalling the devastating foot-and-mouth disease outbreak among Saskatchewan cattle eight years ago, told a congressional subcommittee that the Canadian government still is not alive to the full dangers of the new threat posed by heavier foreign shipping on the great lakes.
In a report of subcommittee testimony published today, Donald Fletcher, executive secretary of the rust prevention association at Minneapolis, said the U.S. needs Canada's full co-operation in stepping up port inspection work to block foreign pests and disease.
"I am sure we will get it," he said talking of Canadian co-operation, "but they just do not understand the dangerous possibility yet."
The report goes on to quote Mr. Fletcher as saying further:
"Canada has the attitude that they are more interested in what is going out rather than what

Supply-Agriculture
is coming in. They are inspecting their ships for insects and diseases and have the proper sanitation of the grain going out. I have been at meetings attended by top quarantine people of Canada and their interest is definitely in the export trade. They fail to realize that they get some of these animal diseases and insect pests which may cause trouble to their producing areas."
I also have a clipping here of an editorial written on this subject. It is headed "Negligence in import inspection". Other editorials dealing with this question have been written.
I should like to assure the house that Mr. Fletcher is speaking, apparently, without being aware of the facts, and that there is no validity in the allegations he has made. I wish to outline what the actual situation is with regard to the prevention of disease and pests harmful to plant or animal life in Canada. We have in effect an extremely thorough inspection service to look after this matter, and I regret very much that a considerable number of people in Canada should have been perturbed and alarmed over this report which, as I say, has evidently been made without the gentleman concerned being aware of the facts.
The government, through the Department of Agriculture, has for many years been cognizant of the danger of introducing foreign animal and plant diseases and plant pests through foreign imports and foreign shipping. With respect to animal diseases, veterinary port officers have been maintained for many years at ocean ports.
Prior to the opening of the new St. Lawrence seaway, all foreign vessels entering the Lachine canal and existing waterways serving a route identical to the St. Lawrence seaway were boarded and examined by port officers operating under the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
With the development of the St. Lawrence seaway, it was recognized that the dangers of introducing foreign diseases would be increased. Fully one year ahead of the opening of the seaway negotiations were opened to establish a system of boarding and checking each vessel entering the new seaway. All vessels docking at Canadian ocean ports are boarded and all foreign garbage is either retained in enclosed containers on board the vessel or is removed and incinerated under the supervision of a departmental officer. All vessels arriving at or docking at the port of Montreal and entering the St. Lawrence seaway are required to have all garbage removed and incinerated under departmental supervision.
In addition, all vessels entering the St. Lawrence seaway are inspected for foreign meats included as ship's stores. Where such foreign meats are found they are sealed in

the ship's locker with a departmental seal. The master of the vessel must sign a statement, available in 16 languages, that no garbage is to be dumped in Canadian waters.
An Animal Contagious Diseases Act certificate of clearance listing the foreign meats aboard, the government seal numbers on the locker, and the ports of call both Canadian and United States of the vessel within the St. Lawrence seaway and the great lakes is issued to the master. Copies of this certificate are forwarded by mail to the Canadian and United States port veterinarian for each port of call of the vessel. In the case of Canadian ports of call, the vessel is checked at each port to assure that departmental requirements are being met. Also, at certain designated Canadian great lakes ports garbage is removed and incinerated under supervision.
All this is required under the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and violators are subject to prosecution. While this entire operation at the entrance of the St. Lawrence seaway is carried on by Canadian government officers of the department's health of animals division, veterinary officers of the United States department of agriculture are kept informed, and the program was developed in consultation with them.
With respect to plant pests and plant diseases the department, through its plant protection division, has for many years maintained port inspection officers at all oceangoing ports. With the opening of the new St. Lawrence seaway, inspection under the Destructive Insect and Pest Act has been provided at all seaway ports where foreign plant cargoes are permitted to be off-loaded.
In addition to requiring import permits and closely checking each individual shipment of plant material, attention is paid to the general cargo for evidence of all insect pests. For the purposes of both the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, departmental fumigation stations are maintained at Halifax, Nova Scotia; Saint John, New Brunswick; Quebec city and Montreal, Quebec. At other ports where fumigation services are needed, commercial fumigation units are used.
I thought it was desirable to make a fairly complete statement in connection with this matter in order to reassure Canadians who have been disturbed over this report. Particularly as it mentioned the foot-and-mouth outbreak in 1951, which caused a great deal of damage as far as the Canadian cattle and livestock industry generally is concerned. I should like to repeat that I regret very much that a statement of this kind was made without knowledge of the facts. I think our inspection service is as thorough and painstaking

as any which exists anywhere in the world. In fact most of the complaints we get in connection with it is that it is too thorough. There are some who are prevented from bringing things into the country because of our very strict regulations.

Before proceeding with my remarks in connection with these estimates I want to say on behalf of this group that we appreciate the good work that is being done by the staff of the Department of Agriculture at the headquarters in Ottawa, at the various experimental stations and throughout the country. I might say that until quite recently there were several members of this staff who were old classmates or college mates of mine, but they have all retired and vanished from the scene. I am the only antique member of that generation gyrating around here at the present time.
I want to say that the study of the agricultural development in Canada is to me fascinating. I have read the history of this country from a number of sources, and I have always found it interesting. I think possibly that is because I come from pioneer stock. I have known what it was to take two dozen eggs to the store in a lard pail

in order to get a package of tobacco and two boxes of matches. I therefore speak from experience as a pioneer settler. I have a keen appreciation of the problems of the smaller ranchers in particular.
However, the history of agriculture in this country is a most interesting study, dealing as it does with the early settlers in Quebec, in the maritimes, then later in Ontario, then along the coast of British Columbia and Vancouver island, then later the settlements in central British Columbia and in the southern interior valleys with which I am most acquainted. These valleys were settled by people who in the early days principally supplied the local market for beef, dairy products, small fruits and vegetables. That local market has been destroyed in recent years by certain influences in this country. The hon. member for Vancouver East will deal particularly with that problem later this afternoon; my remarks are going to be somewhat general.
This settlement in the interior valleys of British Columbia included many types of people, some with experience and some without. In any event they were sturdy, happy pioneers of many races, including a good number of people from our neighbour province of Quebec, who went out there in the early days. Those valleys were settled by people who were attracted by the climate, the scenery, the fishing, the hunting and their hope, at least, of the opportunity of making a reasonable living in good circumstances.
In following the hon. member who has just spoken I want to mention this matter in order to show the close relationship this group has with Canadians of French descent, and our appreciation of their problems. I enjoyed the speech made by the hon. member who has just spoken. I want to say that the district from which I come is extremely interesting in that respect. When David Thompson discovered the Columbia river, his boats were rowed by Canadians of French descent. The first agriculturist we had in the Arrow lakes area was an old gentleman of French descent by the name of Nels Demers who stayed in that country alone, after the Hudson's Bay Company left, from 1866 until such settlers of whom I am speaking arrived in the early days of this century. I cared for that old gentleman prior to his death. He was the first agriculturist in the area. I am glad to say that we have two small communities named after him, namely East and West Demers. I knew a gentleman of French Canadian descent who was also a small rancher and was the first shipbuilder in the area; he was named Blondin. As a matter of fact a creek that flows through my ranch is 79951-0-215J

named after him because of our friendship and our great respect for him. Those were happy pioneer days. Conditions are entirely different today.
I cannot help living in the past on occasion. I knew another Canadian of French descent who was an early pioneer rancher and a prominent Liberal. One day just prior to the 1945 election he said to me, "I am president of the Liberal association and I work hard for my party, but I want to tell you this. We have known one another for nearly 50 years and I am praying like hell for you". I won the election. Hence I have had some valuable assistance from my constituents of French descent.
I am coming around to my general theme in a few minutes. Anyway, some of these people arrived with capital, some with small assured incomes; but as to others, the only assets they had was grit and the determination to succeed. All of them, whether they were of British stock or not-and I may say, in case anybody does not know, that I came originally from the old country-had a sense of humour; they were fond of animals, particularly horses, and some were overfond of the ladies. But this combination of settlers from Britain and people coming from French Canada built the farmer and co-operative movement; it was the foundation of the cooperatives which developed in connection with the fruit industry of British Columbia.
I mention these things to show what can be done on the basis of mutual co-operation and understanding. When I hear all this talk about Quebec and Ontario and British Columbia, from my point of view it seems to be all tommy-rot. As far as I am concerned we are all Canadians first.
There are, of course many different types of Canadians, and before I proceed I might mention, in order to illustrate the difference in these types, that a Kootenay rancher is entirely different from those to be found in other parts of Canada. For the first ten years when some people occupied the land, they kept the farm. Afterwards, with experience they became ranchers and graduated to the point where the farm kept them. On one occasion a dear old gentleman asked me to go and see his cows. He had been a secretary-valet to a well-known noble lord in Britain and had come out to this country to settle. He was a Christian gentleman with a great love of animals, anxious to learn all he could about farming. He had attended a meeting addressed by some official of the federal department of agriculture, who told him that if he wanted to get the greatest possible milk production the cows had to be kept comfortable. The more comfortable they

Supply-Agriculture
were, the more milk they would produce. One day he came to my place in the middle of the winter-we had a cold spell and the temperature was one or two degrees below zero, a somewhat unusual occurrence in our part of the country, I must say-and asked me to come and see what he had done to keep his cows comfortable. He had commanded his wife to make up blankets to cover the animals; then he had contrived something after the fashion of tea cozies which he used to cover the udders. Then he finished the whole thing off by having puttees very nicely made out of sacking. When I had admired all this he asked me, "After all that, don't you think I should get more milk?" I agreed with him.
I mention this to illustrate the various types of settlers we had at that time. Those were different days. The wants of the pioneers were simple and costs were low. They were catering, on the whole, to local markets which were growing at that time, the mining industry and the developing forest industry. Today the situation is entirely different. We have machine production, high capital investment and high costs. One cannot go on the prairies now and get 160 acres and start farming with an expectation of getting anywhere. Nor would it be of any use attempting to begin with the small amount of capital which once was sufficient. A high capital investment requires abundant credit, and we are increasingly dependent on export markets. In British Columbia this is particularly true with regard to the marketing of fruit and other commodities.
Agriculture is without doubt in a crisis, and I am of the opinion we are not going to solve the problem in Canada if we treat it on a partisan basis. This group makes its contribution in this house with respect to agriculture in an effort to find some common and satisfactory solution. I think we should not underestimate the difficulties and complexities in the changing industrial society in which we are living-
You are not speaking for your group, but for yourself.

The hon. gentleman does not realize that I am expressing a general approach to agricultural problems on behalf of our party this morning.
There is no doubt that we face a serious crisis in agriculture in the years ahead unless there is some appropriate action and leadership by federal and provincial governments. In a democratic society they must give some leadership in the right direction. First, in our opinion, we have to decide the place and value of the family farm in our society. I am a great believer in the family

farm. I am one of those persons who deplore human beings becoming robots and I recognize, as do the other members of this group, the values which have sprung from family farms and rural communities throughout the generations in the history of this country.
In this connection I should like to quote from a book which I have been reading and which I have found most interesting. It is called "The Failure of Success-The American Crisis in Values" and the author is Esther Milner. I advise anyone to get a copy who is interested in studying the circumstances under which we live and the problems we face at this time, problems which cannot be solved by short-run methods. I want to quote from this book, because I am one of those who do not see everything as black or white, whether in regard to international or domestic affairs. I believe that in a democratic society all sections can make some contribution to the solution of any problem, whether it is unemployment or farm markets or the maintenance of the family farm, providing democratic governments give some leadership and thought to the problem. On page 17 there is a passage in this book which reads as follows:
I find it the colossal irony of our times that the hostility of the two major antagonists on the world scene originates in their mutual commitment to the same philosophic fallacy, the doctrine of "economic man." Both the United States and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics espouse social ideals of the highest order, but in practice the leaders and the people of both countries believe that the economic aspects of man's life are not merely of primary but of ultimate importance. Our disagreement lies essentially in our insistence that our own economic system is the better pathway to the goal-but the goal is essentially the same: "On both sides it is asserted that the only, or at any rate the main objective of nations should be industrial prosperity. This is implied in the dogma of economic materialism, which forms the basis of both these systems, ostensibly opposed as they are.
I think there is a lot of truth in that statement. The subquotation continues:
"And as these theories merely reflect the state of public sentiment, industry, which was formerly regarded as one means to a higher end, has become the supreme end for individuals as well as for whole societies."
Although the writer of these words was speaking of what at his time were two economic theories only, his words have proved more prophetic than he could have realized. Emile Durkheim wrote these words in the 1890's, twenty five years before the formation of the U.S.S.R. and nearly sixty years before our current international stalemate.
I have read that paragraph, which I think is most informative, to indicate that our attention must be directed to several problems in our society, and that the economic problem is only one line of advance toward a solution. In my opinion the improvement and development of the family farm offers

an opportunity to preserve the traditional values of our society, to preserve a contribution of real value while at the same time stabilizing at a satisfactory level the economic position of our farmers in a changing, industrial society.
In saying this I am not overlooking economic security for all groups in our country. In dealing with these questions as parliamentarians, with possibly the greatest responsibility of any parliament in our history, we have to move ahead on a number of parallel lines of which economic improvement is only one. However, one of these lines is a program that will provide economic security for our farmers.
Conditions have developed rapidly since the termination of world war II, and there is no question but that the policies of federal and provincial governments have been unrelated in a number of fields. I am not criticizing the emergency measures which have come into being to meet the problems of depression, war, inflation and drought. The major problem now is surpluses. In view of this group the measures have been emergency, piecemeal and unrelated to one another. There is no evidence of a planned over-all national policy based on a long range approach to economic and sociological facts.
I am not blaming individuals or particular governments. To some extent governments, organizations and individuals are victims of circumstances that have arisen in recent years. But there is no evidence of a sound approach to the genuine happiness sought by all mankind. This is not found purely in the pursuit of monetary values. Happiness embraces a contentment in the pursuit of a useful occupation, a love of nature and satisfactory relations with human beings.
On the one hand government and research workers, to whom I give all credit, are devoting themselves to knowledge and methods which increase production and surpluses and at the same time depopulate the farms and rural communities. Other government agencies are providing credit to apply this new knowledge and these new methods to an expanding production. On the other hand the federal government, with price supports and deficiency payment policies, is limiting production. We have this agricultural team pulling in opposite directions, with the horse representing the scientists going ahead but the horse representing the marketing policy sitting back on its haunches. There is contradiction in over-all agricultural policy that is difficult to avoid without planning. The problems this creates increase daily. A number of small farmers are unable to make a living through failure to adjust to these

changed circumstances. They cannot meet the forces at work as the result of our lack of an over-all agricultural policy.
I have never accepted the philosophy of the worship of bigness, size or quantity. I know there is an attraction to large scale industry, huge production and size in anything. I have known a man to enter a room full of ordinary people, and when it was whispered that he was worth $10 million it seemed to establish an aura around him. People are hypnotized by wealth, numbers and size, which in my opinion represents an unsound approach to life, instead of being hypnotized by character, intelligence and industry. However, that is all part of the evolution of the capitalist society.
Of course we do not see things in black and white. There has to be some common ground between the extremes if there is to be a solution. We can learn from our past history and from the practices of the present in other countries.
We find a lack of concern for agricultural human resources. Some people are not fazed by the thought of doing away with the number of farmers. This is accepted by people without thinking of the impact on our society and the contribution made by farmers to our national development. I have met many farmers. Many are without clear objectives and a sense of direction. They are confused by the fog of the circumstances under which they live. I think it is also fair to say that many farm organizations lack over-all agreement as to the policies best suited to correct the situation, but all agree on the value of the economic family farm. That is a good starting point on which they all agree. They feel that because of its value the family farm should be preserved.
In that connection I want to quote briefly from the brief of the interprovincial farm union council presented to the federal government on February 17, 1960, the second paragraph of which states:
We believe that an agricultural industry based on the concept of the family farm can best serve the national interest of Canada. To maintain the industry on this basis requires a clearly defined agricultural policy.
On October 14, 1959, addressing the farm equipment institute's 66th annual meeting in Montreal, Quebec, the Minister of Agriculture, Hon. Douglas S. Harkness, stated as follows:
"The agricultural policy of the Canadian government is designed to ensure that the average economic producer will secure a standard of living comparable to that of people in other industries, and thus ensure a healthy agriculture, with sufficient production to meet our own needs and those of export markets."
Under the combined circumstances of rising farm costs and declining farm prices, we submit that the realization of this stated objective cannot be attained.

I support this question posed to the government in the brief:
Are federal agricultural policies to be enacted that will aim at the preservation of widely distributed private ownership of productive assets, enabling men to maintain themselves and their families on their farms, or does the federal government intend to let those economic forces have free play, that encourage the trend to anonymous, corporate ownership with all its inherent dangers?
There is a general realization among farming people and others in Canada that the family farm is a necessary productive unit in our society, because it has proved its value.
What are we going to do about the problem? I said that farmers lack purpose and direction, and that farm organizations have failed to agree in general on a solution to the question. Federal and provincial governments lack accord with respect to a common policy. We also have disagreement among individual farmers because of differences in their experience or training and the circumstances under which they live. This great industry is drifting in a sea of day to day expediency on the part of government, farm organizations and farmers themselves. All have been forced into this state of expediency because of the lack of planned over-all national policy for agriculture related to the facts and the circumstances of our time.
I pay tribute to what is being done; I do not underestimate it. I recognize the value of the marketing legislation that has been passed by governments as the result of prodding by agricultural organizations. I recognize the value of the credit facilities provided by the federal government and some provincial governments. I recognize the value of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which has done a great work in that field. I recognize the value of the Praire Farm Assistance Act and the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act. However, all this work that is being done on a piecemeal basis is based largely on expediency so far as the federal and provincial governments are concerned. I wish to pay tribute to those who conceived these policies and have given effect to them, and also to those who have responsibility for administering them. However, Mr. Chairman, in our opinion a satisfactory and effective long term, sound agricultural policy can result only from research into all the facts, and we lack that. You cannot design a satisfactory policy without knowledge, without the facts.
As I said before, I pay tribute to our scientists in the agricultural service and in universities who are engaged full time in meeting day to day problems, whether in the field

of production, marketing and so on. But what is required-our farmers' organizations have touched on it to a limited extent up to now and I think the agricultural institute of Canada has been dealing with this question possibly in more detail in recent years-in the opinion of this group is an independent farm policy agency. We need the facts; we need some organization to get the facts, to get the truth-not propaganda, not opinion, but the facts-upon which to base for a number of years a satisfactory national agricultural policy. We need the facts with respect to land available and land resources, the productive capacity of this land, the markets, the transportation and all the other factors, shall I say, that relate agriculture to the rest of the community.

We suggest this because we believe the more governments secure the co-operation of the organizations representing the farmers and of other governments on as wide a scale as possible, the sounder will be the approach in a democratic society. We believe that such a foundation should include representatives of governments, both federal and provincial; it should include representatives of the agricultural institute of Canada, which is a professional organization of registered agriculturists in this country, with a lot of good men in its membership and a lot of experience gained throughout the years; it should include representatives from the staffs of the universities and representatives of the farm organizations. I suggest in that group of persons you have a

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose for the luncheon adjournment I had been mentioning some of the things said by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska. In his remarks he made some comparison of prices with reference to the time that the previous administration was in office but what he failed to mention was the fact that from 1950 onward prices of these products steadily declined and production compared with consumption rose very sharply. He said that government members were complacent about the agricultural situation. I should like to tell the hon. member that we are not, that members on the government side who represent rural constituencies are no more complacent than anyone else. We know there is a problem but we do know that the government, the first in a long time to do so, is making an honest attempt to find a solution under a very capable and honest minister.
During the Easter recess I drove some 1,200 miles through my constituency in central Alberta and talked to farmers, elevator agents, municipal and county authorities and small businessmen. The 1959 crop, a very small percentage of which was taken off during the harvest season last year, was coming off quite well with the exception that losses in the amount of production amounted to about 20 to 25 per cent and losses in quality were about the same. As a result farmers were harvesting less than they would have got if harvesting had been normal.

I would not say that they were discouraged because they feel that the government will look for some method to assist them. Farmers who took off their grain during the last harvest season had grain that was in a damp or tough condition and they have suffered losses for that reason. I think there is a very real need at the present time for some type of assistance. I have been getting letters constantly from the farmers union of Alberta and the locals in my constituency, all of which make the same plea that I have made before and repeat today. I think it is time for the government to consider very seriously repeating the acreage payment that was made in 1958, namely $1 an acre to a maximum of 200 acres. I feel this would afford real relief at a time when it is most needed. In the area I represent the farmers average 300 acres or less. This means that these people need assistance, particularly in view of the fact that they have suffered a partial and in some cases very substantial loss so far as their 1959 crop is concerned.
I should also like to bring to the attention of the minister and the government an idea which has been put to use in the United States. I read about it this morning in a publication of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and I think the government should give some consideration to it. I have here the news and information bulletin of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and on page 5 there is reference to the United States conservation reserve program under which an annual rental running from $11.53 to $11.75 per acre is paid.
We have in Canada, particularly in the west, areas that have been in crop production for a good many years and where a conservation reserve of this type would enable the replacing of valuable soil elements which constant production has taken from the land. We also have areas which at one time were in forest and are now under agricultural production but which I think could well be reforested. We have great hopes, of course, with respect to the new department of forestry which it is proposed to set up because in that area millions and millions of feet of lumber used to be produced. That production has now disappeared and our lumbering industry has also disappeared with it. I would hope that the government would have a look at this conservation reserve program and the taking out of production of land which has been farmed so long and also land which is basically not suited to agricultural production.

On March 4 when these estimates were introduced into the house the Prime Minister had this to say on agriculture, as found at page 1766 of Hansard:

I wholly subscribe to the views expressed in that quotation and, as applied to the agricultural situation in the maritime provinces particularly, I think that every effort should be made to stimulate agriculture.
This is a point about which I feel very strongly. I have already said in this house, and I repeat at this time, that if we ever find a solution to the agricultural problems which exist in the maritime provinces we will have gone a long way toward the solution of the unemployment problem in that area. This farm specializes in the growing of grasses and grain, exactly the things in which the farmers in my area are interested. I wonder how many of my farmers have ever taken the trouble to even visit that farm? I would say that at least 95 per cent of our local farmers do not even know where Nappan is. Mr. Chairman, like all hon. members, the minister has a general interest in all affairs which affect the Canadian economy but because of his position in the cabinet he of necessity has a particular interest in the problems of agriculture. It is because of his position as Minister of Agriculture that I should like to take this oppor-

Supply-Agriculture
tunity, on the first item in his estimates, to ask both for his consideration of and comments upon a problem which in our estimation, because certain policies have been allowed to go unchecked, is proving a serious detriment to agriculture directly, to the agricultural industry not quite so directly, and is indirectly affecting all other aspects of our economy and business itself.
I have mentioned this particular problem briefly during this session and now, when there is an opportunity to discuss it with the Minister of Agriculture, I should like to go into it in a little more detail. I have reference to a dual policy which up until now has been allowed to go completely unchecked by either this or the previous government. I refer to companies outside of Canada, in particular companies in the United States, being permitted to purchase outright fruit and vegetable canneries in this country and to close them down as far as all operations are concerned, thereby blocking out completely the purchase of Canadian agricultural produce, blocking out completely the employment of Canadian workers and, as far as their operations are concerned, the opportunity of Canadian consumers to buy produce grown and processed in Canada.
I know for a fact that this policy has been in operation for some time in British Columbia, in Ontario and in at least one important place in the province of Nova Scotia. United States companies have bought out Canadian companies and have closed up the industries, retaining only two things, namely the incorporation and the name brand. It is now the practice of those United States companies to process the production outside of Canada, to can it outside of Canada, to ship it into Canada and then place a Canadian brand name on the product. I gave some examples of that in this House of Commons some three weeks ago where fresh frozen strawberries sold under the well-known Canadian brand name of York were not Canadian. They came in one instance from the United States and in the other from Holland. I gave a further illustration of tomato juice being sold in Canada under a Canadian name brand but which was produced and canned in the United States.
I say there is a general application of the policy of United States companies buying out Canadian companies and following that procedure.
There is also another policy which has gone unchecked about which I have not made mention before. Well known, long established large wholesale distributors within a province are being bought out by large financial and chain stores who, after the purchase, operate them wholly and solely under their original

names and original brands. That is, they follow a practice along the same lines as that which I have previously mentioned. Goods produced outside this country are processed outside this country and then sold in this country under the known provincial brand, although most people do not realize that those companies no longer operate under the original ownership but are part and parcel of big financial interests and financial chains.
I say this is a problem in Canada. It has resulted in a loss which I am going to estimate as being in the neighbourhood of many, many millions of dollars to our agricultural producers and to the industry which necessarily follows success in agriculture.
I know this is the general effect across Canada, but I want to speak in particular of the province of British Columbia of which I have the honour to be one of the representatives in this house. In the past the Fraser valley has been, among other things, famous for its production of strawberries, not only for the consumer market when they are picked fresh but also for canning and frozen purposes. That situation no longer exists. To a great extent that marvellous production of the past is now dead because of the two policies I have just mentioned and because the canneries no longer exist. Instead of strawberry jam and fresh frozen strawberries from the famous Fraser valley being sold under the York brand we now get imports from the United States and Holland. To me there is something blatently nonsensical about that situation.
But let us go on to something that, important as the strawberry crop is, is of even greater value to the people of British Columbia. In that regard I wish to refer to the world famous Okanagan valley which I maintain is one of the finest areas not only in Canada but in the world for the production of fruits, small fruits and vegetables. Until a few years ago there were 15 or 16 large canneries operating in the area from Lillooet on the north down the Fraser to Lytton, Ashcroft, Kamloops and Chase and in the actual Okanagan itself at Vernon, Rutland, Kelowna, Summerland, Oliver, Keremeos, Osoyoos and Cawston.
Today there are only two vegetable canneries left of any size and I am informed by the operators that the operations of the remaining two are declining rapidly. Why? Not only was this a marvellous area and can continue to be for the production of beans, beets, pumpkins, asparagus and so on but it was also a wonderful tomato belt. These canneries operated not only because of these other vegetables but were primarily required for the processing of tomatoes. However, because of the two policies I referred to a few

minutes ago there are now only two canneries operating and their operations are diminishing. This has come about because of the purchase by United States interests of our canneries in British Columbia and the fact that they have closed them and because of the purchase of the wholesale distributing companies by national chains and big financial interests who have done this for some reason or other although they claim they love Canadian enterprise. They are importing agricultural products from outside our country with the result that the agricultural producers of British Columbia and the industries associated with agriculture have suffered very severe losses.
Surely the reduction from 16 canneries to two shows what has taken place. I admit that until some two and a half weeks ago I did not know how serious the impact was. I received by air express cans of tomato juice purchased by a citizen in the city of Vernon in the heart of the Okanagan and the tomato growing region. I do not know how well the Nabob name is known in eastern Canada but it is certainly known in western Canada. There was a can of Kelly Douglas tomato juice packed in the United States by Nabob. Then there was a can of Malkin tomato juice. The Malkin name is as well known in British Columbia as Nabob or Kelly Douglas. Again this was tomato juice packed in the United States for the Malkin company of Canada. Yet this tomato juice was being sold in the city of Vernon where one of the remaining canneries is located. The president of that company, in a letter to me which is not marked confidential, informs me that on the basis of his lifelong knowledge of the Okanagan and the industry as a producer and packer it is his conservative estimate that the policies about which I am now complaining are resulting in a direct loss to Okanagan agricultural producers and labour of not less than $5 million annually.
I know that the minister has at least some interest in this matter because the information branch of the department issued a release on the 14th of this month and I should like to quote from it.
The agricultural stabilization board has been authorized to provide assistance to the growers of tomatoes in British Columbia in the form of a payment of $8 per ton for No. 1 cannery tomatoes and $5 a ton on No. 2 cannery tomatoes marketed from the 1960 crop, agriculture minister Douglas S. Harkness announced today. Mr. Harkness said the assistance, which has been provided to British Columbia tomato growers since 1958, would not be extended after 1960.
He noted that while B.C. tomato production had been subsidized by assistance payments of $109,000 in 1958 and $38,000 in 1959, the contracted tomato acreage in the province had declined by more than 50 per cent between 1957 and 1959. Further, while
Supply-Agriculture
B.C. tomato production represented only about 6 per cent of the Canadian output of processed tomato products, the producers in other areas have been able to carry on their operations without assistance under the stabilization act.
He stated that under these circumstances continued government subsidies to B.C. tomato growers could not be justified. Assistance had been approved for 1960 only for the purpose of permitting producers to make any necessary adjustments in their future plans, and support under the stabilization act would not be available after this year.
It is quite obvious that is the end of assistance as far as the tomato growers of British Columbia are concerned. But, Mr. Chairman, the date of that announcement was the 14th of this month and my information from the producers and canners of the Okanagan is that April 14 was too late to make this known to them and that they cannot do any planning now for the increasing of acreage or with a view to reopening any additional canneries. They say that not only is it too late now for anything of major significance to be done to bring back that segment of agriculture in the Okanagan but the fact that the door will be closed after this year is a further blow.
I know that all of us are grateful that there is going to be some assistance this year, but what did it amount to last year- thirty eight thousand dollars. The important issue is, what is contemplated by the minister and the government to reclaim agricultural production and cannery operation so far as tomatoes are concerned, to name just one field? If we lose out as far as tomatoes are concerned then we will also lose so far as the production and canning of other vegetables is concerned. All that is left, therefore, is the fresh vegetable market.
When we have statements made, I would take it by very responsible officials of Boul-man's Limited that they are losing out now to the extent of over $5 million a year as a result of this policy of foreign ownership, control and incorporation but selling under Canadian brand names, then I think we who are interested in the development of agriculture in Canada and processing in Canada as well as consumers being able to support products which are grown and processed in Canada through their purchases, should ask the minister at this time what consideration he has given to the impact of the two policies about which I have been speaking for these past 15 minutes; what interest he has shown in them and what action he is taking or contemplates taking to renew and revive the agriculture and canning industries in Canada. This problem not only affects British Columbia and Ontario, but within the last three weeks I have found that the system is now going into effect in Nova Scotia.

Supp ly-A griculture
This is a creeping disease which has to be stopped and only the government can do it. I realize there are many difficulties in the way. I realize there are many problems, but they will have to be tackled, even if it means going to the extent of charging for the use of the brand name of Canadian companies which are bought up and closed out and using that money to assist agriculture in other directions. If we are going to have outfits like Kelly Douglas doing what I say they are doing, and about which I got the evidence sent me by express the other day, then they too will have to be made to contribute in some way or other toward the assistance of agriculture in other directions.
If no policy is going to be laid down to recapture what we are now losing, then I say this is indeed a serious matter and something which should never have been allowed to go unchecked as long as it has. I sincerely hope the Minister of Agriculture will have something to say about this, some good and constructive information to give us as to his policy for the protection and enlargement of agricultural development along the lines I have been mentioning.

Mr. Chairman, it may seem strange to many that I, from the far north and the far west, should rise in this committee to speak on agriculture. Apart, however, from what was said about the dominion experimental farm at Haines Junction, Mile 1019 on the Alaska highway, some years ago, there has not been a word said in the house or in committee about agriculture in the Yukon since the Yukon has had a seat in this house. I propose, first, to deal with the possibilities of mixed farming in the Yukon, and to make a few suggestions as to how this can be achieved. I also admit freely at the outset of these remarks that I am certainly no expert on agriculture, nor a farmer. The information I have gleaned -has come, however, from experts and from those who are undoubtedly acquainted with agricultural problems in the north. I will be making remarks about certain negative attitudes on the part of government administrators in the north in so far as the development of agriculture there is concerned.
Agriculture has an important part to play in the development of the Yukon. People, wherever they are, must eat. Virtually all the foodstuffs consumed in the Yukon must be shipped in from the outside. In addition to the climatic severity, Yukon residents are penalized by a certain isolation from the rest of Canada. Modern facilities for travel and communication have reduced this isolation factor to a minimum, but the high cost of importing food still remains. Much will be done

to alleviate this with the increase in the development of agriculture. A thriving local agriculture industry in the Yukon could supply much of the beef, pork, poultry, eggs and common garden crops now consumed there. With proper management it would be possible to supply local markets with fresher and higher quality produce. Eliminating the roughly 1,500 mile freight haul from outside points would result in a saving to the Yukon consumer both in quality and in price. There would be less danger of food shortages brought on, for example, by longshoremen's strikes at our only port of entry on tidewater at Skagway, although there is the port of Haines which is seldom used.
Agriculture would also lend stability to the economy of the country in this way: Farmers are generally good citizens. They attempt to build homes for their families and businesses for their sons. They must keep abreast of the -times in order to survive, and in doing this they show an interest in their community and in the country as a whole. The permanent settlement of the Yukon could be aided considerably by agricultural development. Of lesser importance, yet nevertheless significant, would be the labour required for the building up of farms. There would be a demand for such skilled labour as carpenters, heavy duty operators, mechanics and, later, a demand for unskilled labour.
Much of the native population, now more or less unemployed, could be utilized as unskilled labour on the farms as they develop. Work on or about farms would give natives a chance to obtain better food and living conditions than they now enjoy, and heaven knows the standard they are now experiencing is low enough. With some training and experience gained working on farms some Indians could very easily become good farmers. This could work in well with the government's program of training the Indian people. At present those people interested in agriculture are apt to be a bit scarce. There are, now, only two possible sources of such men. One source would be the natives who have worked on farms, both private farms and the experimental farm. You might find some natives, also, amongst those who have worked for the big game guides who would be interested in livestock production. The second source would be the native schools.
The men from the first mentioned source would be older and better able to judge whether farming could hold their interest. They may also be inclined to let things slide along the way they are and look to the government for support whether or not they work. The group from the schools would be younger and would learn more easily. They

might be given encouragement and counselling before leaving the schools. The government, in co-operation with private farmers, could select a few likely candidates and introduce them to the art of farming. It might be possible to work out some scheme whereby the government could give the farmer some assistance with wages and the farmer could supply room and board and training for these natives, in much the same fashion as the on the job training that has been provided by the Department of Labour and the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
If this proved satisfactory the natives, after becoming basically familiar with life on the farm, could be given additional training in agriculture. It is unlikely that there would be sufficient interest at first to justify an agricultural school in the Yukon, but interested students might be sent to schools such as the Olds and Vermilion schools of agriculture in Alberta. If there were sufficient interest, various short courses in agriculture might be instituted for the special training of these natives. Courses in mechanics and machinery maintenance were given at the Alberta school of agriculture to Indians and Eskimos from the Northwest Territories.
I believe that local farmers would be willing to co-operate in such a program. Most of these hire some native help during the heavy work periods. While the farmer is unable to afford year-round unskilled labour he would have work enough or be willing to train a native if he had some assistance with wages. If candidates that were genuinely interested in agriculture were selected for such a training program, they could become quite successful farmers. If a few natives got a start in farming it is unlikely that others would not follow their example. Such a program could be of great assistance in solving the native problem in the Yukon. It requires co-operation, I would suggest, between the two departments.
Agriculture in the Yukon is an economically sound venture and is advantageous to the country as a whole. Before I rose to make these few remarks one or two of the hon. members in the chamber here tempted me by saying that all we could produce in Yukon was perhaps onions, potatoes and a few stunted trees. I took it as a joke because I know those who make such remarks are joking and that they have not been to Yukon in order to see for themselves.
One of the sources or in fact the main source from which I am obtaining the technical information which will be following in my remarks is from one of two brothers who operate a farm in the Yukon called the
Supply-Agriculture
Pelly ranch. The brother with whom I correspond and of whom I speak and from whom I get my information is a gentleman by the name of Hugh Bradley who is a Bachelor of Science having graduated from the University of Alberta and the other brother is a graduate of the agriculture school in Vermilion, Alberta. These two lads have farmed in the Yukon since 1954, have kept very accurate records of their production and have formed a few ideas, many of which I will be stating here, on how agricultural development should be going in the Yukon. So when I say that agriculture is economically sound, I am not just stating a possibility or a thesis; I am stating a fact because there are economic farms in the Yukon but they are having their difficulties.
Why then are there not more farmers in Yukon? One reason is the lack, among people who may be interested, of knowledge of conditions and opportunities in the Yukon. Most Canadians still think about the Yukon in the terms of the writings of Robert Service, Jack London, Rex Beach and the like. Much has been done recently to publicize our part of the country but much remains to be done. We are endeavouring to sell Yukon to the rest of the country and we must do so if Canada is to derive the advantage of her development.
Our territorial government in the Yukon, in my view, should show some positive action in this direction. In the past the attitude of both the administrative and legislative bodies has been apathetic or negative. Our chief administrator, known as the commissioner of the Yukon Territory, let it be known on several occasions that he thought and still thinks that any attempt at agriculture was and is foolishness and that assistance would have to come from the federal Department of Agriculture. With this latter part of the commissioner's statement I agree but with his negative attitude toward the development of agriculture in the Yukon I most emphatically disagree. Official encouragement could possibly have influenced private individuals in years past to start farming in the Yukon. Official endorsement and aid would certainly have helped. That official endorsement and that official aid has not been forthcoming and has yet to be forthcoming.
If no interest is shown by the local government so-called-and I call it local government so-called because there is still much to be done in the way of leadership by the commissioner and those about him-why then should we as a federal government be interested? Nevertheless, the federal government was sufficiently aware of the need to establish three experimental farms in northern Canada. The station we are concerned

Supp ly-A griculture
with is at Mile 1019 on the Alaska highway and is now an experimental farm. Results of experiments carried out on this farm are available. These reports clearly show that an agricultural enterprise in the Yukon is possible; that crops will grow; that livestock will survive and multiply; that garden crops can be produced. The continued existence of private farms and results obtained at the experimental farm show that agriculture is feasible from an economic standpoint as well.
The territorial government should be interested in the development of agriculture and indeed it has expressed that interest in the session of last year-in 1958-when they passed a resolution calling for federal financial assistance in the setting up of a committee to assess the agricultural possibilities in the Yukon and the methods of developing the area. To my knowledge no federal action has been taken on that request of the Yukon legislative council. The present council is showing great interest in the development of agriculture, but this has not been so in the past. The council could assist in many ways. The cheapest form of assistance would be an information service. There could be a main source of supply from which people who may be interested could obtain information. There should be a main source from which people could obtain estimates of amount and location of land, costs and prices, climatic conditions, production data as far as is known, populations, markets, regulations governing the sale of farm products, taxes and licences required and many other factors. To obtain such information now you must trot from one department to another all over the federal building in Whitehorse and finally end up at the office of the chief administrator who, I informed the committee a moment ago, is the commissioner and who thinks it is all foolishness. Our commissioner just does not know or just does not care to find out.
The territorial and federal governments should be interested enough in the development of the country to assist in road building to agricultural areas. Many of the best areas for farming are now rather inaccessible. It will be rather difficult to encourage settlement of these lands unless there is some promise of accessibility. Agriculture is just as much a resource as are the mineral deposits in the land. The government is making great strides in opening up and making accessible mineral land. The same approach should be made to the opening up and making accessible of farm lands.
The federal government should be able to do something about the most deplorable situation which exists with regard to obtaining agricultural land. This situation is in a

terrible mess. Picture, if you can, a farmer who wishes to commence his operation in the Yukon being faced with the requirement to pay $30 an acre for his land before he can commence farming. It should be possible to arrange some terms for deferment of taxes and purchase price until the farm can become established. Much of this might be beyond the jurisdiction of the territorial government, yet they should be heard on the subject. They are in a position to bring certain pressures to bear on the proper agencies. They should at least try.
Of direct assistance to farmers the federal government might undertake the following projects in the Yukon:
1. A caterpillar tractor of no smaller than D-6 size with equipment for land-clearing and breaking should be made available for the use of farmers. The government could in the interests of agriculture supply the "cat" and transportation for it. The farmer could cover the cost of the fuel oil and the operator. Such a program would have to be planned in advance so that the machine could be used to the greatest advantage. Work in each area would have to be arranged so that the "cat" would spend a maximum amount of time working and a minimum of time in transit. This program might be patterned somewhat after the project of the Alberta government in farm land clearing in the Wanham area of the Peace river district.
The land clearing project would have to be administered by the government. In this regard there is need for a full time extension man in the Yukon. I would suggest an employee of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources with an extension office located at the experimental farm at Mile 1019. Location at the farm would to best, since such a man would have to work in close co-operation with the Department of Agriculture. This man could administer the plan mentioned earlier in regard to natives in agriculture. He would organize and administer land clearing projects and land settlement. He could also report to the farmers the findings of the experimental farm and advise the staff there on new research projects farmers would like to see undertaken. Another part of his job could be the planning and planting of lawns and gardens in the Whitehorse area.
Another way in which the government could aid farmers is in connection with freight subsidies. For example, the cost of freight on fertilizer amounts to about $130 per ton. High freight costs such as these virtually prohibit the use of fertilizers and limits the use of livestock and poultry supplements. Freight nearly doubles the price of farm machinery in the Yukon. Such a situation

does not encourage agricultural enterprise. Most provincial governments give some aid along these lines to settlers in fringe areas. Some such program should be instituted to aid Yukon farmers.
A fourth form that government aid could take is indirect, but it would be of great benefit to the Yukon farmer. I am referring to realistic support of the experimental farm. I am not criticising what has been done. Much valuable work has been accomplished, but there are some fields that have been neglected because of insufficient technical staff. It has been ten months since the tragic death of the farm superintendent at mile 1019. This seems an over long time for even the civil service to find a replacement. The position should be re-examined and if necessary reclassified to make it sufficiently attractive to interest and hold a high calibre man, since it is a position of utmost importance to Yukon agriculture.
Perhaps it is because of the recent reduction in the isolated post allowances that it has been difficult to find a man to adapt himself to life and work on the experimental farm. If this is the case, it must be deplored that the interdepartmental committee on isolated post regulations found it necessary to recommend such a reduction in this allowance.
The field of animal science is the most important field to Yukon agriculture yet there has been no technical staff in that field there long enough to do any important research. The new superintendent might well be an animal science man. My understanding is that the person who will be going to take over the farm at the end of this month is a soil expert. If that is so, it is most important that a research officer in animal husbandry be appointed soon. The following topics might be suggested for research in this field: research in pastures; the best species or mixtures to use in planted pastures; carrying capacity of planted and native pastures; assessment of native pastures from both carrying capacity and nutritive standpoint; best management practices for tame and native pastures; livestock insect pests. Winter feed: hay planted versus native; species yields and nutritive properties; relative merits of hay; straw and bundles for winter feed; study of mineral and vitamin supplements that may be necessary when using local feeds; silage for winter feed. Is silage the way to beat the unfavourable haying season we have? Is there sufficient moisture in our crops to make good silage? What crops and mixtures can we grow for best silage? Housing: do cattle significantly do better when they receive warm housing? Can open shed housing be used satisfactorily? What about housing
Supp ly-A griculture
against black flies in summer? Research in hogs, poultry, dairy cattle and sheep-these would come as minor projects and are listed in order of importance. The reason they would be of secondary importance is their relatively larger demands for concentrates which are harder and more expensive to produce.
Climatic conditions make crop production alone a marginal venture, but in conjunction with livestock production it is important. Any research which will lead to production of more and better feeds will be most helpful. Variety trials should be continued. Field management experiments should be expanded, since there is much to be learned about rotation, fertilizers and tillage practices in relation to the north. There is room for work in drought tolerant and frost tolerant varieties. Farmers will want to know the best methods of breaking and preparing land in this area, also to what extent irrigation will be economical. Forage research is very important. We have only one legume that is dependable, and even it has serious drawbacks. Much more selection and breeding work is needed. Some attention need be given to introduction and adaptability of new species. There should be experiments with silage under our conditions.
There should also be sufficient staff on the experimental farm to permit off-station work. Crops and practices suitable for the Whitehorse area may not be suitable for Mayo and Dawson city. As more farms are established more off-station work will be required. It would be an advantage to have information available for the use of prospective settlers. It is important to have some correlation of meteorological data. To illustrate the variability over the territory, Dawson city has a frost free period of 78 days; Mayo, 64 days; Snag, 51 days; Watson Lake, 85; Whitehorse airport, 78. Undoubtedly there will be a wide variation in precipitation, and mean temperature conditions should be investigated near all centres of population and in as many good farming areas as possible.
Horticulture may not be of prime importance to farmers, yet more people will be growing kitchen gardens. There should be research along these lines. Farmers will be interested in easily grown horticultural crops such as potatoes. Early drought tolerant varieties adapted to Yukon conditions should be produced.
It is hoped that the federal government will see that the experimental farm has sufficient staff to carry out these and other important research projects. There is a large investment in land, buildings and machinery, a very large investment; now let us have personnel to turn out some badly needed information. Of prime importance, perhaps

Supply-Agriculture
before any of these things are undertaken, should be a careful assessment of the available arable land in the Yukon.
The future of agriculture will depend greatly on the development of the rest of the territory. The Yukon will never become primarily an agriculture area. However, farming will be a basic industry. Even the present population would benefit greatly by the presence of more farms. As the population increases, so will the need for farms increase. Yukon agriculture should aim at the production of high quality produce. In the future there will likely be an outlet in Alaska for our produce. To ensure maintenance of quality, to protect producers and consumers, the government should institute inspectors and inspection services as soon as possible. There should be restrictions on imports to protect the growth of the industry. Diseased potatoes have already been imported from Alaska. This could seriously injure any future potato production in the Yukon.
The relative isolation of the Yukon and of farms in the Yukon will make it possible to grow highest quality seed for export. Isolation is required for the production of cross-pollinated forage seed. In dense farming areas it is almost impossible to plant pure varieties because of this. The Yukon could make much use of this feature.
Longer hours of daylight in our northern latitudes favour flower and seed formation. For example, Russian wild rye grass will not head out and set seed in North Dakota because of shorter days. It seeds well in the Yukon, so in the future a good export business may develop. Winter hardiness of crops which will survive in the Yukon will be another selling point. There is a strong possibility of exporting seed to countries of similar latitude in Europe. To go along with this idea, seed production is favoured by mixed farming and the Yukon will most surely be a mixed farming area.
In the future there will be smelters in the Yukon. Many by-products of smelters are converted into fertilizers. Fertilizers alone form a large part of the income of mining companies. A ready market for their byproducts would be a help to smelters and a source of fertilizers near at hand would be a help to farmers.
Storage facilities, slaughter houses, inspection services, expanded markets will all go together to ensure that the Yukon consumers get fresh, top quality locally raised produce. We will be able to break an egg in the frying pan and be reasonably certain that it was laid this year. As the Yukon grows so will farming grow.

All this points to a healthy, more stable economy and to the need for a greater understanding and appreciation of the development of Yukon agriculture both at the federal level and more particularly at the administrative level in the Yukon. There must be something more at the administrative level, at the level of the commissioner, in the Yukon. There must be leadership at the administrative level in the Yukon to ensure that this development will occur. There must be the will to encourage agricultural development. There must be a strong desire at the administrative level in the Yukon to assist in that development. Negativism must be banished. There are great possibilities in the Yukon for the development of agriculture and if the Yukon is expected to support a large population in anticipation of the development of industries in the north, then planning should commence now and not ten years hence for the development of an agricultural industry which will sustain that population.
