A few weeks ago the Prime Minister said something about the agricultural policy of the government and the statements he made interested me very much, especially when he referred to that portion of the policy which he enunciated in 1959 to the effect that the government was engaged in a comprehensive study and review of the Canadian Farm Loan Act as a means of meeting the small farm problem, etc. Then he went on to say, and I quote from Hansard of March 4, 1960 at page 1766:
We believe that agriculture is one of the most important sectors of the Canadian economy; that the prosperity of agriculture is an integral part of Canadian prosperity; that governments do have a responsibility in a constructive and effective manner to strengthen Canadian agriculture for in doing so the economy as a whole is strengthened. We believe that the national interest can best be served if we endeavour to do our utmost to develop efficiently and economically our resources, including agriculture; that farmers should have continuing opportunities to earn sufficient income to enjoy the benefits of our rapidly growing economy and the rising standards of living enjoyed by the population as a whole; and that a reasonably high and stable level of farm income is an essential prerequisite to a high level of employment and income in Canada generally.
We take the stand, and have, that government action to help Canadian agriculture to help itself is in the Canadian tradition of self-reliance and that government action primarily designed to provide and round out opportunities for farmers to do well on their own is a desirable objective.
Some of the agricultural problems are national in scope while others are regional. The policies that we have followed have been designed to deal with problems where they occur.
I do not think anyone would quarrel with a policy designed to deal with problems where they occur, be they national or regional, but what about the implementation

of this regional policy enunciated by the Prime Minister? The district of Thunder bay has yet to benefit from such policy.
I complained on several occasions at the lack of consideration for the farmers of the Fort William district. The Prime Minister said in effect that the Canadian Farm Loan Act would be amended to better facilitate assistance to small farmers. It seems to me that it is not so much the revision of the act that is important-the name was changed, I believe-but rather the implementation of the act by the officials in the field. That is what is important.
I have said previously and I say again that unless a farmer in our district has sufficient collateral to show it is next to impossible for him to secure a loan to enable him to develop efficiently and economically the agricultural potential of his holding. For some years there has been considerable discontent among the farmers in the lakehead area, the Thunder bay district. Many Thunder bay district farmers had a very difficult winter following one of the poorest growing seasons in many years. Grain crops were 62 per cent below those of 1958. The decreased harvest was estimated as a loss of $300,000. Some farmers did not have sufficient crops to make harvesting worth while. A great number were forced to buy feed for their cattle. Potatoes and other crops were also down, leaving farmers with little revenue with which to purchase feed.
Last year the hon. member for Port Arthur and myself suggested to the minister that a meeting be held between federal and provincial members of parliament and representatives of the federal and provincial departments of agriculture and interested farmers to discuss problems peculiar to the district. Unfortunately, while we did suggest a date we received nothing but a scant response from the minister.
Subsequently we asked for specific information on our region and finally we received a copy of a summary and conclusions designed to strengthen the position of agriculture in the district of Thunder bay. We were told that these conclusions were arrived at with considerable difficulty which necessitated on the ground investigation. It was readily found that one of the great and primary advantages of farming in this particular district was the expanding of the local market which is located at a considerable distance from other farming areas.
The total population of the Thunder bay district is approximately 140,000, of which less than 6 per cent are farmers compared with an estimated 12 per cent for the whole province of Ontario.
Supply-Agriculture
With a distinct federal and provincial farm policy, supported by long term loans, this region could be developed into one of the best garden areas of Canada, especially if the government were to initiate an immigration policy designed to attract suitable immigrants who would undertake to settle on the land. I have advocated such a policy ever since I was elected to parliament, and I have found no sound argument here to induce me to change my view on the situation. Indeed, I am now more than ever convinced that such a policy would be beneficial to the whole of Canada.
Another great advantage which would stimulate farming in this area is that although grain production is very limited, with the great source of livestock feed at the local terminal elevators, it could become a No. 1 livestock producing area of Canada. The distance from marketing facilities could be overcome with the adoption of an equitable freight rate structure. The present structure militates against the farmers having a fair chance to compete with primary producers of the west and east.
It is true that the area of improved farm land is comparatively small; it is approximately 70,000 acres. The reason the area is no larger is the freight rate discrimination which I have already mentioned and the apparent indifference of our senior levels of government in not giving this district a fair chance to develop.
Our present farmers are concentrating on dairy products, poultry, eggs, potatoes, and so forth. Of course, there are other products, but in the main these constitute the bulk of products from which our farmers make a living. There is a great potential for expansion in fluid milk, potatoes, vegetables, greenhouse products, small fruits such as berries of all kinds, mushrooms, poultry, eggs, turkeys, honey and feeder cattle. The establishment of feeder plants for cattle and hogs near our terminal elevators should be considered as a distinct advantage to the area.
I know that most people in Canada, including a great many hon. members in this house, have the conception that Thunder bay is a land of timber and rocks. Thank God, we have rocks, beneath which there lies the pre-Cambrian shield, which is rich in minerals of all kinds; but make no mistake, we have thousands of acres which could be under cultivation now, but because of a lack of promotion and interest is worthless bush. Seventy per cent of the total farm area is unimproved land, compared with 39 per cent for the province of Ontario, and

Supply-Agriculture
only 20 per cent of the total occupied land is under crops, roughly one half of the provincial average.
I say to this government, give us help to establish large cold storage facilities; establish a meat and crop grading station. This is one of the things that the farmers of my district have asked the federal and provincial governments to establish for a long time. The answer to our problems have invariably been the stock answer: farming is not sufficiently developed to warrant the establishment of these facilities. How can we develop our potentials if the government continues to ignore the needs for such development?
If this government is consistent in its promises and statements to the effect that farmers in ever part of Canada will receive the same consideration, it should practise what it preaches. I admit that the farmers in my constituency cannot compete in numbers or in wealth with the farmers of the west or of the east. It seems to me, therefore, that precisely because of these deficiencies the government should extend no less consideration to them in evaluating their needs. I suspect that one of the reasons why they are neglected is that they are not organized like a trade union. They are more of a rugged individualistic nature, but that is no reason why they should be forgotten.
Last year the interprovincial farm union council presented a brief pertaining to policy research. They advocated the setting up of an independent research agency to help in providing farmer organizations with the information for sound decisions in matters of crops, marketing, and so forth. This was to be an independent government research agency to help solve problems of agriculture. I wish to quote from page 3 of this document:
The objectives of this research would be: to explore the underlying principles of agricultural policy; to examine and place in perspective the peculiar features of the Canadian economy that are significant for such policy; to establish sound bases for developing and applying economic policies; to appraise particular current policies in this field with the object of suggesting alternatives or recommending changes; and to make the results of such research widely available, especially to farmers governments and the general public.
On page 6 it goes on to describe the scale of research activities and says:
While it would be desirable to start such research on a substantial scale there are good reasons for establishing a modest organization in the beginning to permit it to be developed on a sound basis as it expands. It should be emphasized that if the maximum benefits are to accrue to farmers, governments and the general public, it would need to be so organized as to be capable of logical expansion to meet policy research needs.
It is proposed therefore that the research organization be established with a nucleus staff of researchers, a small clerical and stenographic staff, a

moderate allotment for office and travel funds, and a small allotment to be used for grants to colleges or universities where such may be needed to obtain the supplementary information required by the research agency.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in their presentation to the cabinet on February 24 of this year, made another plea for such a research council. They recognized the need for a study of farm problems and included in their presentation was this passage which I wish to quote:
There is a keenly felt need today for expanded research both into farm marketing and into the more general economic and social problems facing the farmer. Such research is needed so that we may intelligently develop and improve our marketing and support programs. It is needed also so that we may better understand what is happening in the farm economy and to rural society, and in doing so learn to develop farm policies and extension programs that will better meet the needs and problems which agriculture faces.
I fully agree with the establishment of such a council. Indeed, I urge the minister to give consideration to the implementation of this request. But in all of this there is not a word on behalf of farmers of the kind we have in northwestern Ontario. I suggest that if such a council is established it should have a member from the district of Thunder bay, one who would be familiar with the problems peculiar to the district, and that the council should not be just for the exclusive benefit of the wheat farmers of western Canada.
I come now to one of the most important features necessary for the development of the farming communities of our district, and that is an adequate system of providing funds without which farmers cannot expand nor can new farms be developed. Up to the present the experience with the farm loan board has not been the happiest so far as the farmers of the Thunder bay district are concerned. Recently I expressed the hope that the farm credit corporation, successor to the defunct farm loan board, will be more amenable in its policy toward small farmers and would-be farmers desirous of establishing themselves on the land because up to the present it has failed to establish an equitable policy of farm assistance for areas such as northwestern Ontario. However, hope springs eternal. What is needed is a policy of liberal credit and a national agriculture policy designed to encourage ownership and operation of farms in every section of Canada.
Finally, I wish to appeal to the minister to give the lakehead area some consideration. I suggest that he and some of his departmental assistants pay a visit to the Thunder bay district. The minister would be astounded and it would be an education for him. I

suggest that such a visit would stimulate interest in the development of our land and it would also serve as a valuable encouragement to those who are already established in our rural communities.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that we will be proceeding with private bills in about 20 minutes I thought I might reply to some of the comments and speeches that have been made this afternoon. I thought that the hon. member for Kootenay West made a very good speech. He stated that agriculture has been going through a difficult period due to changed conditions and the technological revolution that has taken place in agriculture particularly during the past 15 to 20 years, and that a partisan approach will solve nothing from the agricultural point of view. I thought that was well said by the hon. member for Kootenay West and I was very glad to hear him say it. I am only sorry that some of his colleagues were not here to hear him say it.
There is no question that agriculture has been going through a difficult period during the last 15 to 20 years. Everybody concerned with agriculture knows that that has been the situation. Everybody knows that during this period a very rapid mechanization of agriculture has been taking place. Great improvements have been made from the scientific point of view in feeding methods, in breeding and so on. All of these things have combined to produce in the western countries at any rate a surplus situation so far as a large number of agricultural products are concerned with the result that during the past 10 years particularly we have had increasing difficulty in disposing of the agricultural products that we have been able to produce. In other words, production has been going ahead more rapidly than the ability to find economic markets for these products has developed. This is a situation in which we are likely to be for some time, at least during the immediate future.
All of this has created quite a different set of circumstances from those which prevailed in the past and has made it necessary for us to change our thinking very materially as far as agriculture is concerned. Unfortunately the thinking on agriculture of a considerable number of people has not kept up with the changes that have taken place. They are still thinking of the past when it was possible to operate a farm of comparatively small acreage and provide the family with a living which would at least support them in a reasonable way. That day is now past.
The standard of living existing in this country is very much above what one might call the peasant level and therefore small
Supply-Agriculture
acreages which in the past were capable of supporting a family are no longer capable of doing so on the basis of anything like the standard of living that is demanded in a country such as Canada at the present time. From the point of view of economic family farm units this makes it necessary to form considerably bigger units from the acreage point of view and particularly from the capital point of view, involving livestock, machinery and so on, than was the case even as little as 15 to 20 years ago.
The hon. member for Kootenay West said that there was a great contradiction in our agricultural policies because on the one hand the scientists were constantly working to produce better breeds of livestock, better types of plants and improved methods of producing agricultural products of all kinds- in other words, we are doing a great deal of work to encourage and increase production-* while on the other hand marketing policies to quite an extent were designed to limit production. I would point out that these two lines of activity are not necessarily in contradiction of each other. If we are to have successful farmers they must be able to produce in as efficient, scientific and up to date a way as farmers in any other part of the world, and in order to put them in the position where they can do so we have to continue to develop our research activities and to ensure that these activities produce the best types of both plants and animals for particular localities and evolve the best methods of producing agricultural commodities of all kinds. In view of the sort of situation we have at the present time, where in most of the western world agricultural products are being produced in excess of the ability of the people to consume them, it is necessary to have production and marketing policies which will keep production down to the limits of what can be marketed or disposed of in an economic way.
We can, of course, give away a certain amount of our products in certain areas. Canada has done a great deal of that, but there is a very definite limit to what can be done along that line. By and large we have pursued policies which, as I say, ensure, so far as that can be done, that very large surpluses which cannot be disposed of are not piled up with consequent storage costs and so on.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska made a speech, but I do not believe I will say very much about it. His speech was of the type, as the hon. member for Kootenay West said, which did not carry forward the cause of agriculture in any way. It was a purely partisan, political speech. It was designed to show that the situation

Supply-Agriculture
of the farmer was better under the previous Liberal government than it is under the present Conservative government, something which it is impossible to do. Every farmer knows that this government has done far more in the way of putting schemes into effect or passing legislation to aid farmers in the two or three years which it has been in office than the previous government did in the 10 or 15 years before that. As I say, I do not think I should take up any time in dealing with the very large number of, what shall I say, false assumptions and misinformation which the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska put forth.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin spoke of a scheme being carried on in the United States for taking land out of production, the soil bank as it is called there. I should like to point out that we have done a fair amount along this line in Canada. We have set up the P.F.R.A. community pastures and provincial community pastures in western Canada, a means by which land has been taken out of ordinary production, out of grain growing, and made available for the use of smaller farmers to pasture livestock, thus enabling many people who otherwise would not be able to diversify their activities to get into the livestock business. The conservation measures which we are presently carrying out, and which we contemplate carrying out to a greater extent in the future, will involve more work along this line.
The hon. member for Kent, (N.B.) quoted some figures by which he attempted to show that the deficiency program in connection with eggs had led to a decline in production from the small producer rather than the large producer. Of course, our great trouble had been overproduction. The statistics used were from a paper which has been a most bitter opponent of deficiency payments on eggs. I do not know where this publication obtained these figures, but as I say the paper has been the bitterest opponent of this program in connection with eggs. Actually our records, taken from the grading stations, indicate the exact opposite. A big reduction in egg production has taken place in so far as the large producer is concerned. I think every logical examination of the matter would show that was what was most likely to take place, and I think that is what has taken place. Actually this same publication from which the hon. member quoted these statistics complained for several months that this policy was going to destroy the large egg producers, the most efficient producers. Now, evidently, this publication is trying to be on both sides of the fence in connection with this matter.

The hon. member for Kent, (N.B.) spoke of the necessity for disseminating the results of agriculture research to the farmers so that they can make practical use of it. I agree with that thoroughly. It is essential that improvements which are discovered by scientists at research stations be communicated to the farmers, the men who can actually make use of them. We, of course, do a considerable amount of work along that line by making the results of our research work available in pamphlets of all kinds which are distributed particularly to agricultural schools and tc the provinces. As the hon. member knows, education is the exclusive prerogative of the provinces and, in so far as agriculture is concerned, the division of the work between the dominion and the provinces is that the provinces are primarily responsible for the dissemination of agricultural information to the farmers and we are primarily responsible for the research work, the discovery of new methods, new types of plants, better types of livestock and so on.
The hon. member for Vancouver East made a speech dealing particularly with the fact that United States firms, in recent years, have been buying up Canadian canning plants and closing them down. He dealt particularly with the tomato situation in British Columbia. I should like to assure him that I was alarmed at both of these situations, and I had an investigation made in order to ascertain what the situation was. In so far as the allegations which have been made about United States companies buying up Canadian plants and then shutting them down, are concerned, this is what the investigation showed. In so far as Ontario is concerned, whilst there has been a considerable amount of buying up of small canning plants by large United States canning concerns, the total amount of production has not been reduced. In many cases what happened was that three, four or five small and comparatively inefficient canning plants were bought up and one big canning plant with a large production, greater than the four or five, was built or one of the bigger plants which had been bought was greatly enlarged in order to make one large, more efficient operation. In British Columbia there has been a definite reduction in the number of canning plants, but that is a different story which I shall mention later.
Production as a whole, so far as the canning of fruits and vegetables in Canada is concerned-I have not got the report here- has not been materially reduced as the hon. member for Vancouver East seems to believe.

I think the only way to see the whole story is to look at the complete figures. If you go into a store here or in British Columbia you will find that for the most part the goods are Canadian. However, you will find some that have been canned in Italy, England and all other countries. However, the bulk have been canned in Canada.
So far as the tomato situation in British Columbia is concerned, the difficulty there has not been a matter of United States plants buying up British Columbia canning plants and then deliberately closing them down, the difficulty has been entirely one of economics. The cost of producing tomatoes in British Columbia had risen too high to enable them to compete with tomatoes canned in the United States or other areas. There are several reasons for this. The first one is that the tomato acreages in British Columbia were quite small. They were too small to be worked by machinery and, therefore, a great deal of hand labour was involved.
The second thing is that labour has become increasingly hard to get in British Columbia and increasingly expensive; I refer to farm labour. Hence the cost of producing tomatoes in British Columbia has gone up out of proportion to the cost of producing them in Ontario and particularly out of proportion to the cost of producing them in California.
The most important factor of any is that, as a result of soil deterioration in British Columbia, both the yield and the quality of the product has gone down. It is owing to lack of organic material, to a large extent, in the soil which they have not been replacing as they should have done. As a result, the yields of tomatoes in British Columbia at the present time are just about 50 per cent of what they are in California. It is quite clear that if you are producing only half as much of a product on an acre of ground in one place as is being produced in another, you cannot compete. The actual fact is that the growers in California have been getting an average of $10 a ton less for their tomatoes than have the growers in British Columbia. But nevertheless, in spite of that fact, the growers in British Columbia have been steadily driven out of the business; they have not been able to compete because they were growing only half as many tomatoes per acre.
Supply-Agriculture
These are the basic and essential reasons why the tomato canning industry in British Columbia has been getting smaller and smaller and, it appears, is not going to be able to continue as an economic industry in competition with tomato growing either in Ontario or in California. No one regrets more than I do that that is the situation.

No. Apple production in British Columbia is still being carried on in a fairly successful way and also the production of other tree fruits of various kinds. But as to tomato growing and tomato canning, the chief vegetable canning business in the Okanagan and adjacent valleys, as the hon. member indicated, this is what has happened. You are better off spending the same amount of money on an industry which shows some sign of being capable of being improved or revived or of being made successful.

The answer to that statement is that we do so. What the hon. member seems to want is special consideration which is not extended to farmers anywhere else.

Supply-Agriculture
The government does not build cold storages for farmers at any place. We make a subsidy to a farmers' co-operative or to a commercial concern that wants to build a cold storage. The same thing applies with regard to a cheese factory. We do not build any of these things. The farmers themselves or some commercial concern in the area must go ahead and build; under these circumstances we provide subsidies but we do not build them. I think perhaps the hon. member was under a misapprehension in that regard. I should like to assure him that we give or are prepared to give to the farmers in the Thunder bay district the same consideration as that accorded to farmers anywhere else in the country.

I have a comment or two to make in respect of this particular bill and the situation surrounding it, the evidence leading up to the petition being presented, and certain other material considerations which arise in the evidence presented before the Senate committee.
As the petition indicates in the first paragraph, the marriage between the petitioner and the respondent took place on September 27, 1952 in Montreal. The allegation of adultery is made in the petition and it is stated that the respondent committed adultery on September 16, 1959 with a person whose name and address is given. The petition states further that the respondent and the corespondent lived openly together as man and wife, and there is evidence given in support of these statements. I may say that there are no children born of this marriage; consequently this is a case with regard to which I do not run any risk of falling foul of the rulings made governing the committee in so far as references to children are concerned.
The petitioner was sworn and at page 9 of the evidence testified that she was married, where, by whom, gave her husband's and her own religion and was shown a document which she identified as the church certificate of her marriage. Some evidence was given about the problems existing prior to the alleged adultery. At page 10 Mr. Leithman, counsel for the petitioner, examined her as follows:
Q. Now, witness, following your marriage to your husband did you live together as man and wife?
A. Yes, we did.
Q. Are there any children?
A. No, sir.
Q. When did you and your husband stop living together as man and wife?
A. About September, 1957.
Q. Will you tell this honourable committee under what circumstances you left. Tell the committee just what happened.
A. Well, as you know-
Q. Just speak to the committee.
A. -I worked, and came home from work about nine o'clock in the evening and found my husband in bed with another woman. He put up quite an argument, and I left and stayed at my sister's for the night. X came back the following night thinking he would have a reasonable answer and found all my clothes outside the door, so I never went back.

Q. In other words, he evicted you?
A. That is right, sir.
That is a startling question. I continue:
Q. Can you recall the exact date? Would you repeat the date?
A. September, 1957.
Q. Since September of 1957 have you lived together as man and wife? Did you get together again?
A. No.
Q. Has he supported you since that day?
A. No, sir, I have supported myself.
Q. You have had no relations at all since September of 1957?
A. No, sir.
I assume the reference is to intimate relations. I continue:
Q. Have you any personal knowledge of the alleged misconduct set out with one-?
A. I have never met her.

A. I have never met her.
I am deleting the names of the parties.
On page 11 reference is made to the fact that no collusion or arrangement exist between the parties. The examination of the petitioner by her counsel continues as follows:

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I draw your attention to citation 144 of Reauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition. For some time now the hon. member and his colleague behind him have been following the practice during private members' hour of connecting up a speech or so-called address to this house with lengthy quotations from a document which he has in his hand. By citation 144 and rulings of other Speakers in the past it has been clearly established that the purpose of the rule is precisely to prevent that pattern of addressing the house or the committee. This citation reads:
It is a rule in both houses of parliament that a member must address the house orally.
Certainly I do not think that citation can be stretched to the point where an hon. member may link together extensive verbatim quotations from any document whatsoever with a very few words. I would appreciate very much, Mr. Chairman, if you would consider whether the pattern of addressing this committee in this way is consistent with the spirit of the citation I have quoted.

May I comment on the point of order raised by the hon. member for York-Scarborough. I say first of all I appreciate his drawing of this question to the attention of the committee. However, I do not think we are justified in giving the weight to the point of order raised by the hon. member that he is asking us to do. Citation 144 reads:
It is a rule in both houses of parliament that a member must address the house orally, and not read from a written, previously prepared speech-
Then, it goes on to say:
-for the reason that, "if the practice of reading speeches should prevail, members might read speeches that were written by other people, and the time of the house be taken up in considering the arguments of persons who were not deserving of their attention".
I do not think the hon. member for York-Scarborough would suggest, for instance, that the comments and questions of Senator Roebuck were not deserving of our attention. This is not a previously prepared speech, I submit. In this instance, what it is is substantiation; in other instances it might be argument against the bill. The bill says, "The marriage is hereby dissolved." Therefore, in order to prove whether the marriage took place in the first instance it is necessary to

read from the testimony before another committee, not a previously prepared speech but testimony, to prove that particular allegation in the bill.
In the bill reference is made to adultery. That is the reason why the marriage is to be dissolved. Again, what I am doing is not reading a previously prepared speech but reading evidence taken under oath before a committee of the other place in substantiation of the question of adultery.
If I may reply to the hon. member's attempt to avoid the clear implications of this ruling, he has said that he is not reading a previously prepared speech. That is exactly my point.

On the evidence of Daigneault and Paquette it would appear that there was a frank and open admission that these people were living together as man and wife. This carries with it the implication that intercourse took place between them and probably will continue to take place between them as long as they continue to live together as man and wife. In fact, if this divorce is granted it may provide an opportunity for the respondent and

corespondent to legalize the relationship they have had for some two or three years. I think it has existed for about that length of time but in any event it has been in existence for some time.
There does not appear to be a great deal more to add apart from mentioning the evidence of the petitioner herself. She said that she came home and found her husband in bed with another woman. She came back the next evening thinking that he would have a reasonable answer, found her clothes outside the door and never went back again. It makes one wonder why she did not consider taking action for divorce in September, 1957 when this incident occurred in her own home involving her husband and another woman. I do not know why it took some two years for her to petition for a divorce. That is beyond our knowledge at the moment. One wonders why she waited for two years but apart from that I think we can classify this case as one of those so-called open and shut types of cases where there is no conflict in the evidence given by the two investigators.
Both investigators appear to be fairly sure of what happened so far as time and so on are concerned. That is in contrast to other cases we have had where the investigators were not sure. Because these investigators worked on this case together from start to finish and were both there at the same time I think we must insist that their evidence coincide and not be at variance. After all, they are working together and collaborating. How many members did the hon. member count?
Those who are here are getting very tired of this nonsense.

I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the hon. member for Saskatoon that if he is not careful he will be misquoted again and his remarks will be attributed to someone else as they were the other day. I do not mind his interruption about nonsense.
I think what the hon. member has to fear is that his own remarks will be quoted.

The hon. member is at liberty to do that any time he wishes. For that matter, anyone else can quote them if they wish. This case appears to be one of those open and shut ones. There is not too much argument about it apart from wondering why there was a delay of two years from the time the wife discovered her husband in bed with someone else in their own home. She left and stayed with her sister over night, came back the next night and found her clothes outside the door. She has not spoken to him 79951-0-217

or had any support from him since that time. One wonders why action was not taken then rather than two years later? Mr. Chairman, there are several remarks that might be made about the contribution to the debate we have just heard but more particularly about the poor lady who has come before us to ask for relief. She seems to have been lost sight of in the welter of words that have been read from the proceedings of the Senate divorce committee. Mrs. Lanese, the lady concerned, is 35 years old. She is a receptionist and waitress and as such she falls into the general category of cases that come before us. This is not a place for rich persons to seek relief by divorce. Most of the people who come before us as this woman does are of humble circumstances and most of them are women. She fits into that category.
She is a working woman and was at all relevant times. She came home one evening after working to find that her husband had taken up with another woman. In those circumstances I would think that she would be an object of pity and a person to be helped if some procedure could be found to help her. Years ago the fathers of confederation decided on the procedure and she has followed it faithfully. On September 21, 1959 she signed a petition in due and proper form and it may be found in the case book before us this afternoon.
I suppose when she signed her name on that petition and thought of the relief that would eventually come to her she had no idea that by coming before us she would be treated more miserably and in a more debasing and humiliating way than anybody anywhere else in the world, and in that regard I think, without referring to a particular area, of the debate we had on Wesdnesday last.
That is exactly what is happening here to this 35-year old woman. The record shows no blot against her and no reason why her problem should be flapped around like so much dirty linen in a place such as this. This is the sort of case which has been well handled all the way down the line. The proper procedures that parliament has set up have been used in this case, procedures which some of us have worked very hard to perfect in order that cases such as this would get due and proper consideration.
I will say no more than that, Mr. Chairman. It has been a scandalous state of affairs and if anybody ever had a clear right to come

Private Bills-Divorce
and ask that relief be given in a gentle and considerate fashion rather than in a scandalous and irresponsible manner, it is the woman who petitions us now.

I should like to raise a point of order. I followed very closely the remarks made by the hon. member for Halifax. Although he did not make reference to me, I must assume I am the person to whom he was referring because I am the only person who has participated in the debate so far, although there have been one or two interruptions. The use of the words "scandalous" and "debased" should not be allowed to pass unnoticed. I should like the hon. member to reconsider those particular words as they apply to me because I am sure I am the one to whom he was directing his remarks. I believe those words should not be used in a personal way because the hon. member knows very well, and we have said it I do not know how many times, that it is scandalous this type of action has to come here and be dealt with in parliament. There are so many alternatives which would make it easier for the individual and better for the individual. This is what we are trying to do. If, in the process of doing that, to get them out of parliament, we take up time, we feel it is unfortunately necessary in order to relate the cases as they come before us, whether they be good or bad.
My point of order is that the hon. member should reconsider those words "scandalous" and "debased".

I can assure my hon. friend that I was not using the words "scandalous" and "debased" in connection with his person. I was saying the method was scandalous. I think there is a distinction between the two. I do not want any inference to be drawn that I was making a personal attack on him. It has never been my practice to do that sort of thing in the House of Commons, but I do think the method used is an extremely unfortunate one. The words were strictly directed toward the method and not toward a person in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I want to ask the hon. member for Halifax a question. Would the hon. member say that, as a result of the C.C.F. filibuster here he feels the C.C.F. is setting up a new class consciousness and that the poor people are deprived of a divorce while the wealthy people can still go to the United States?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order; I am sorry but the Chair cannot allow a question of that kind.

During the remarks made by the hon. member for Skeena he said that his objective in discussing these bills in the way he has been discussing them was in order to focus attention upon what he considers to be the unsatisfactory way of dealing with these matters in this committee. Now, that statement, Mr. Chairman, is quite out of order. By his own admission, therefore, this whole practice is out of order. He has said, in effect, that he is not discussing the bills that are before the committee at all for any purpose related to those bills, but he is discussing them for the purpose of changing the procedure by which divorce is handled.
He and every hon. member in this house has an opportunity, in the proper way, of bringing suggestions before this house for an alteration in the procedure.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order; the point of order was strictly related to two words, and as to whether or not they referred to another hon. member. This matter was cleared up so the point of order has also been cleared up.
I merely want to say that the hon. member for Saskatoon has put succinctly and exactly what we are trying to do. I agree with him; that is exactly what we are trying to do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The previous remarks remind me of one of our farm labourers. When I was a little boy he used to tell me that there were more ways of killing a cat than choking it with butter. Probably some of the remarks that have been made here were suggestions concerning alternate ways of disposing of that cat.
This bill is probably the kind of bill that the chairman of the miscellaneous bills committee was suggesting might be lumped into a category that would separate it from some of the bills we have been discussing during the past few weeks. In my opinion, and probably in the opinion of any hon. member who has taken the time to read the evidence, this bill is mild in comparison with many of the others. It may be that it was, in the light of this situation, that the chairman of the miscellaneous bills committee suggested this woman was having a disservice performed for her because we were discussing her particular case.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the fact she brought her divorce to parliament rather than having it handled through the procedures available in some of the other provinces results in the public of Canada being entitled to know about her problem. It is necessary to discuss it, and discuss it in the terms in which it has been reported to us from the committee which had the
[Mir. McCleave.]

opportunity of hearing the evidence. I am pleased, as was the hon. member for Skeena, to learn that there were no children of this marriage. I believe that if our law were different it would be quite possible, because of the circumstances surrounding this marriage and the fact that there were no children, to dissolve this marriage in a much simpler manner than the course that has been followed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order; we cannot discuss the various methods of divorce. We must discuss this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was leading up to the fact that the circumstances surrounding the marriage were discussed on page 10 of the evidence. We find the following question asked by Mr. Leithman:
Q. Will you tell this honourable committee under what circumstances you left. Tell the committee just what happened.
A. Well, as you know-
Q. Just speak to the committee.
A. I worked, and I came home from work about nine o'clock in the evening and found my husband in bed with another woman. He put up quite an argument, and I left and stayed at my sister's for the night. I came back the following night thinking he would have a reasonable answer and found all my clothes outside the door, so I never went back.
It would seem to me, in this particular instance, if the woman was going to get a divorce she might base it upon the adultery of that particular night. However, it seems that this particular offence was condoned, and I suggest, Mr. Chairman-
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes.
Is it not a fact there were no other witnesses at that particular time, and might that not have had a bearing on it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am not so sure that the hon. senators would not have given some consideration, whether or not there were witnesses. I am not too sure about that. But the surprising thing is that the lady came back the next day. She did not really see anything wrong with this procedure. Frankly, if I had been a senator at the time and had been on this committee I would have asked her what they had had the argument about. She said he put up quite an argument. I am not sure what he put up the argument about. Would he not let his wife in bed also or did she want to get the other woman out and he did not, or what was the argument about? It seems to be very academic. Here would be grounds for adultery. If she had wanted to do so she could have gone out and brought in a neighbour. Here is another woman in her bed. It would have been as 79951-0-217J
Private Bills-Divorce strong evidence as we usually get to confirm that adultery has been committed. But no; he put up quite an argument. The committee has not asked about the argument, as I say. I therefore fail to understand just what has gone on. This marriage just did not end at that particular time. There must have been situations and circumstances developing up to that particular night.
Then she left after this argument, but no explanation was given what it was about. I can see many reasons why there would be an argument on that particular night. But I should like to know whether they were the things that I think the argument would have been over or whether they were matters which may have had a considerable bearing on the fact that she did not immediately go out and bring in her next door neighbour and ask her to be a witness to the other woman being removed from her bed or in laying a charge of adultery which could result in this divorce. She came back the next day and I am not sure what she came back for. From reading the evidence it looks as though she came back to move back into the house again but her clothes were outside and obviously she did not do so.

Scandalous, scandalous,
scandalous.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I hear the sponsor of this bill saying "scandalous". I am not sure just what he is referring to. There are a number of things involved at the present moment that are scandalous. One is that the Canadian people are electing their representatives and are sending them to Ottawa to handle this particular bill which obviously should be handled in a court by legal advisers.
Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is scandalous, Mr. Chairman, because we are being asked to consider evidence that was obtained at a subsequent date on an adultery charge, when an adultery charge already had resulted and had been quite obvious because of the break-up of this marriage in the first place. It is scandalous in a number of ways. If the legal counsel had been consulted shortly after this offence took place I would be greatly surprised if they could not have established the divorce at that time.
They could not have done so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The sponsor says they could not have done so. I am just as happy to take somebody's word, that of the sister to whom she went and to whom she probably related the story. That would be almost as corroborative evidence as one would receive from this particular investigator.

Private Bills-Divorce
It would not be in court.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Maybe it would not be in court but we are not in court. We are in the House of Commons debating a bill. I suggest that I personally would be just as happy to accept the evidence given by the sister to whom she went and knowing that probably the other woman was under duress. When she went to her sister I am quite sure she would have told her the story. I think even the sponsor would have given some consideration to that evidence and would not consider it to be unsupported testimony.
But, Mr. Chairman, this is not what happened. Some time went by and detectives were called in. They restated the case. The case, as I understand it, is where the husband has set up a common law alliance and is living with the other woman, and both admit they are living common law. But this happens in 1959, not in 1957 when the original problem developed. I am therefore suggesting there is some discrepancy in that particular. Certainly we are not using the easiest method and providing these people with the cheapest type of divorce bill possible.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is back again to the method. We must stick to this bill. I do not want to be obliged to remind the hon. member again about this matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am sure you will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the reason why I mentioned the matter of costs and some of the discrepancies was the fact that the sponsor, in speaking on behalf of this bill just a few moments ago, pointed out that this was quite an expensive divorce and that what was happening was causing undue expense and undue hardship to this lady in other respects. I am pointing out that if the legal counsel at that time had given advice that I think would have been acceptable we could probably in 1957 have established the grounds for adultery nearly as well as we could in 1959 without the added expense of having detectives and the other things.
Will the hon. member permit one question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes.

Would it not suggest itself that this woman was so poor that it took her a couple of years to get the money together to come here before parliament? Will he
also say whether he is going to vote for the bill at the last minute before six o'clock? If he does not do so and if he wants to talk the bill out, perhaps we could agree that it is six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Timiskaming has the floor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I agree that this case is one in which there is a common law alliance. I should have liked to continue and to point out that this common law alliance does not necessarily constitute adultery; but I will not do so because of the fact that it is all of six o'clock, that we want to see this woman get the divorce and in this case we also want to see the corespondent and the respondent get the redress that they are being given by this bill.

Clause agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When shall the bill be read a third time?
Now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: By leave.
the third reading of the bill.

speechtext:

pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

speechtext: On division.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I want the sponsor to be sure to note that I voted for it.
Motion agreed to, on division, and bill read the third time and passed.
Would it be possible for the Minister of Veterans Affairs or the Minister of Justice to give notice now of what might take place on Wednesday? I know we have a supply motion for Monday and Tuesday.
The business for Wednesday will be announced on Monday night.
